entities.summary: Montanus of Phrygia was a second-century founder of Montanism, a Christian movement that emphasized the work of the Holy Spirit. Born in an unknown location, Montanus was a self-proclaimed prophet who gained a significant following in the Roman Empire. His teachings, which diverged from the mainstream Great Church, were characterized by an emphasis on the role of the Holy Spirit in the lives of Christians. Montanus's movement gained popularity in the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE, particularly among women and those on the outskirts of society. The Montanist movement eventually split into two factions, with some adhering to Montanus's teachings and others rejecting them. Despite its eventual decline, Montanism had a lasting impact on Christian theology and the development of the Western Christian tradition. The writings of Montanus were compiled and circulated by his followers, including Theodotus of Ephesus, who became a prominent Montanist leader. Montanism's legacy can be seen in the continued emphasis on the role of the Holy Spirit in Christian worship and theology, as well as its influence on the development of certain Christian denominations, such as the Anabaptists and the Mennonites. The historical significance of Montanus of Phrygia lies in his role as a founder of a Christian movement that challenged the authority of the Great Church and paved the way for the development of new Christian denominations and theological perspectives.
